description: Marasmus is a severe form of malnutrition resulting from an extreme deficiency of energy and all macronutrients. It primarily affects young children, leading to significant weight loss, muscle wasting, and loss of subcutaneous fat. This condition makes bones prominent and the child appear emaciated.
symptoms: Severe weight loss (less than 62% of expected body weight for age)
immediate_actions: Initial stabilization with F-75 therapeutic formula
Correction of hypoglycemia and hypothermia
Treatment of dehydration with ReSoMal
Correction of electrolyte imbalance
Treatment of infection with broad-spectrum antibiotics
Micronutrient supplementation (excluding iron initially)
Transition to F-100 therapeutic formula or Ready-to-Use Therapeutic Food (RUTF) during rehabilitation phase
age_group: Children, especially those under 5 years old
content:
Marasmus is a severe form of malnutrition resulting from an extreme deficiency of energy and all macronutrients. It primarily affects young children, leading to significant weight loss, muscle wasting, and loss of subcutaneous fat. This condition makes bones prominent and the child appear emaciated.
Symptoms: Severe weight loss (less than 62% of expected body weight for age), Growth faltering, Lethargy, Irritability, Loss of appetite, Chronic diarrhea
Visual Signs: Extreme emaciation, Visible ribs and prominent bones, Severe loss of subcutaneous fat, Muscle wasting (thin limbs), Loose, wrinkled skin, "Old man's face" (sunken cheeks), Sunken eyes, Dry, thin hair

description: Kwashiorkor is a severe form of protein malnutrition characterized by generalized swelling (edema) and an enlarged liver due to fatty infiltrates. It typically occurs when there is sufficient calorie intake but insufficient protein consumption. This condition is distinct from marasmus, which involves a deficiency in all energy sources.
symptoms: Edema (swelling), especially in the legs, feet, and face
Changes in hair color and texture (sparse, brittle, reddish hair)
Muscle wasting (though often masked by edema)
visual_indicators: Pitting edema (swelling that leaves an indentation when pressed)
Pot belly (due to enlarged liver and ascites)
Sparse, discolored, or easily pluckable hair
future_warnings: Permanent physical and mental growth retardation
Organ damage, particularly to the liver and kidneys
immediate_actions: Initiate rehydration with ReSoMal if dehydrated
Administer F-75 therapeutic formula for initial stabilization (Phase 1)
Treat and prevent hypoglycemia (e.g., with 10% glucose solution)
Treat and prevent hypothermia
Administer broad-spectrum antibiotics to treat infections
Correct electrolyte imbalances (especially potassium and magnesium)
Provide micronutrient supplementation (without iron initially)
Transition to F-100 therapeutic formula for rapid weight gain (Phase 2) once stable
age_group: Weaning children to ages of about five years old
who_muac_threshold: < 11.5 cm for children 6-59 months (often masked by edema in Kwashiorkor)
content:
Kwashiorkor is a severe form of protein malnutrition characterized by generalized swelling (edema) and an enlarged liver due to fatty infiltrates. It typically occurs when there is sufficient calorie intake but insufficient protein consumption. This condition is distinct from marasmus, which involves a deficiency in all energy sources.
Symptoms: Edema (swelling), especially in the legs, feet, and face, Enlarged liver with fatty infiltrates, Apathy and irritability, Changes in hair color and texture (sparse, brittle, reddish hair), Skin changes (darkening, peeling, rash), Muscle wasting (though often masked by edema), Failure to thrive, Diarrhea, Anemia
Visual Signs: Pitting edema (swelling that leaves an indentation when pressed), Moon face, Pot belly (due to enlarged liver and ascites), Flaky paint dermatosis (skin lesions), Sparse, discolored, or easily pluckable hair, Visible muscle wasting (once edema subsides)

description: Iron deficiency anemia occurs when the body lacks sufficient iron to produce enough healthy red blood cells, impairing oxygen delivery throughout the body. This condition can lead to symptoms like fatigue and weakness, and if severe, may cause confusion or shortness of breath. In children, it can hinder normal growth and development.
future_warnings: Impaired growth and development in children
Heart problems (e.g., irregular heartbeat, enlarged heart)
Complications during pregnancy (e.g., premature birth, low birth weight)
Increased susceptibility to infections due to weakened immune system
immediate_actions: Iron supplementation (oral iron tablets)
Dietary changes to increase iron intake (e.g., lean meat, seafood, fortified cereals, legumes, spinach)
Identify and treat the underlying cause of iron deficiency (e.g., addressing blood loss, managing digestive conditions)
In severe cases, blood transfusion may be required
age_group: All age groups, with particular emphasis on infants, children, pregnant women, and those with chronic conditions.
content:
Iron deficiency anemia occurs when the body lacks sufficient iron to produce enough healthy red blood cells, impairing oxygen delivery throughout the body. This condition can lead to symptoms like fatigue and weakness, and if severe, may cause confusion or shortness of breath. In children, it can hinder normal growth and development.
Symptoms: Fatigue, Weakness, Shortness of breath, Decreased ability to exercise, Confusion, Feeling faint or lightheaded, Increased thirst, Trouble with memory and concentration
Visual Signs: Pale skin, Brittle nails, Sore or smooth tongue (glossitis), Koilonychia (spoon-shaped nails)

description: Rickets is a condition primarily affecting children, leading to weak and soft bones due to insufficient vitamin D. This deficiency can result from an unbalanced diet or malabsorption, impacting bone development and overall growth. The analogous condition in adults is osteomalacia.
immediate_actions: Administer Vitamin D supplementation (oral or intramuscular) as per clinical guidelines
Provide calcium supplementation if hypocalcemia is present
Offer dietary counseling to improve vitamin D intake
Recommend appropriate sunlight exposure while ensuring skin protection
content:
Rickets is a condition primarily affecting children, leading to weak and soft bones due to insufficient vitamin D. This deficiency can result from an unbalanced diet or malabsorption, impacting bone development and overall growth. The analogous condition in adults is osteomalacia.
Symptoms: Bowed legs, Stunted growth, Bone pain, Large forehead, Trouble sleeping, Muscle weakness, Delayed motor development, Dental problems (enamel defects), Irritability
Visual Signs: Bowed legs, Large forehead (frontal bossing), Rachitic rosary (beading of ribs), Widened wrists and ankles, Craniotabes (soft skull bones), Harrison's groove (indentation in lower chest)

description: Zinc deficiency occurs when the body does not have enough zinc to meet its needs, or when blood zinc levels fall below the normal range. While blood levels are not always a reliable indicator, this condition can affect various body systems including the immune, digestive, and nervous systems. It is a common global health issue, particularly in developing countries.
future_warnings: Stunted growth and development in children
immediate_actions: Oral zinc supplementation (e.g., zinc sulfate or gluconate)
Dietary modification to include zinc-rich foods (meat, fish, legumes, nuts)
Treatment of underlying causes of malabsorption if present
Nutritional counseling
age_group: All age groups, particularly children, pregnant women, and the elderly
content:
Zinc deficiency occurs when the body does not have enough zinc to meet its needs, or when blood zinc levels fall below the normal range. While blood levels are not always a reliable indicator, this condition can affect various body systems including the immune, digestive, and nervous systems. It is a common global health issue, particularly in developing countries.
Symptoms: Increased rates of diarrhea, Impaired immune function, Poor growth and development, Hair loss, Skin lesions, Impaired wound healing, Loss of appetite, Taste disturbances, Delayed sexual maturation
Visual Signs: Skin lesions (dermatitis), Hair loss (alopecia), Poor wound healing, Growth retardation, White spots on nails (leukonychia)

description: Iodine deficiency is a lack of the essential trace element iodine, which is crucial for thyroid hormone production. This deficiency can lead to various metabolic problems, including an enlarged thyroid gland (goiter) and developmental delays, especially in children. It is a significant global health issue and a preventable cause of intellectual disability.
visual_indicators: Goiter (enlarged thyroid gland in the neck)
future_warnings: Increased risk of other thyroid disorders (e.g., thyroid nodules, thyroiditis)
immediate_actions: Initiate iodine supplementation (e.g., iodized salt, iodine drops/tablets)
Recommend dietary changes to include iodine-rich foods
Monitor thyroid function through blood tests
For severe hypothyroidism, consider thyroid hormone replacement therapy
age_group: All age groups, especially fertile and pregnant women, and children
content:
Iodine deficiency is a lack of the essential trace element iodine, which is crucial for thyroid hormone production. This deficiency can lead to various metabolic problems, including an enlarged thyroid gland (goiter) and developmental delays, especially in children. It is a significant global health issue and a preventable cause of intellectual disability.
Symptoms: Fatigue, Weight gain, Cold intolerance, Dry skin, Hair loss, Constipation, Impaired cognitive function, Developmental delays (in children), Intellectual disability
Visual Signs: Goiter (enlarged thyroid gland in the neck), Puffy face, Thinning hair, Dry, coarse skin, Slowed reflexes, Short stature (in congenital cases)

description: Vitamin A deficiency (VAD) occurs when there is insufficient vitamin A in the body, commonly affecting children and women in developing countries. It primarily impacts vision, leading to night blindness and, in severe cases, can progress to permanent blindness.
visual_indicators: Bitot's spots (foamy patches on the conjunctiva)
future_warnings: Increased risk of severe infections (e.g., measles, diarrhea)
immediate_actions: Administer high-dose oral vitamin A supplements according to WHO guidelines
Promote consumption of vitamin A-rich foods (e.g., dark leafy greens, orange fruits and vegetables, liver)
Implement food fortification programs where appropriate
Treat any co-existing infections
age_group: Primarily children and women of reproductive age, but can affect individuals of all ages
content:
Vitamin A deficiency (VAD) occurs when there is insufficient vitamin A in the body, commonly affecting children and women in developing countries. It primarily impacts vision, leading to night blindness and, in severe cases, can progress to permanent blindness.
Symptoms: Night blindness (nyctalopia), Impaired vision, Dry eyes, Poor growth, Increased susceptibility to infections
Visual Signs: Dry eyes (xerophthalmia), Bitot's spots (foamy patches on the conjunctiva), Softening of the cornea (keratomalacia), Corneal ulcers or scars, Complete blindness

description: Measles, also known as rubeola, is a highly contagious infectious disease caused by a virus. It spreads easily from person to person and is preventable by vaccine. The disease typically causes a characteristic blotchy red rash along with other symptoms.
visual_indicators: Blotchy red rash, often starting on the head and moving down the body
Tiny white spots inside the mouth (Koplik spots)
immediate_actions: Supportive care (rest, hydration)
Vitamin A supplementation for children in affected areas
Isolation to prevent further spread
Fever management with antipyretics
content:
Measles, also known as rubeola, is a highly contagious infectious disease caused by a virus. It spreads easily from person to person and is preventable by vaccine. The disease typically causes a characteristic blotchy red rash along with other symptoms.
Symptoms: Fever, Cough, Runny nose, Conjunctivitis (pink eye), Feeling achy and run down
Visual Signs: Blotchy red rash, often starting on the head and moving down the body, Tiny white spots inside the mouth (Koplik spots)

description: Mumps is a highly contagious viral disease caused by the mumps virus. It typically begins with non-specific symptoms like fever and headache, followed by characteristic painful swelling of the salivary glands. While usually mild, serious complications can occur.
visual_indicators: Painful swelling around the side of the face
Swollen and tender salivary glands under the ears or jaw (unilateral or bilateral)
future_warnings: Meningitis (inflammation of the membranes surrounding the brain and spinal cord)
immediate_actions: Supportive care for symptoms (e.g., pain relief, fever reduction)
Rest
Hydration
Isolation to prevent spread (highly contagious)
Vaccination (MMR vaccine) for prevention
content:
Mumps is a highly contagious viral disease caused by the mumps virus. It typically begins with non-specific symptoms like fever and headache, followed by characteristic painful swelling of the salivary glands. While usually mild, serious complications can occur.
Symptoms: Fever, Headache, Malaise, Muscle pain, Loss of appetite, Tiredness
Visual Signs: Painful swelling around the side of the face, Swollen and tender salivary glands under the ears or jaw (unilateral or bilateral)

description: Rubella, also known as German measles, is a mild, vaccine-preventable viral infection. It often presents with a rash, fever, and swollen lymph nodes, though about half of infected individuals may not show symptoms. The most significant risk is to pregnant women, as infection can lead to miscarriage or severe birth defects in the baby.
symptoms: Rash (starts on face and spreads to body)
Joint pain (especially in adults and young women)
visual_indicators: Rash (starts on face and spreads to body)
future_warnings: Congenital Rubella Syndrome (CRS) in the baby (if infected during early pregnancy)
immediate_actions: Provide supportive care for symptoms (e.g., rest, hydration)
Isolate infected individuals to prevent spread, especially from pregnant women
Recommend MMR (Measles-Mumps-Rubella) vaccine for prevention, particularly for women of childbearing age
age_group: All age groups, with significant risks for fetuses during pregnancy
content:
Rubella, also known as German measles, is a mild, vaccine-preventable viral infection. It often presents with a rash, fever, and swollen lymph nodes, though about half of infected individuals may not show symptoms. The most significant risk is to pregnant women, as infection can lead to miscarriage or severe birth defects in the baby.
Symptoms: Rash (starts on face and spreads to body), Mild fever, Swollen lymph nodes, Sore throat, Fatigue, Joint pain (especially in adults and young women), Itchy rash (sometimes)
Visual Signs: Rash (starts on face and spreads to body), Swollen glands

description: Whooping cough, also known as pertussis, is a highly contagious bacterial respiratory infection. It typically begins with cold-like symptoms, followed by severe coughing fits that can last for weeks or months, often ending with a characteristic 'whoop' sound during inhalation. This disease can be particularly serious and life-threatening for unvaccinated infants.
symptoms: High-pitched whoop sound during inhalation after coughing
Apnea (pauses in breathing, especially in babies)
visual_indicators: Periods of not breathing (apnea) in infants
Cyanosis (bluish skin due to lack of oxygen) during severe coughing
future_warnings: Hospitalization, especially for infants under one year old
Weight loss and malnutrition due to vomiting and difficulty feeding
immediate_actions: Administer appropriate antibiotics (e.g., macrolides like azithromycin) to reduce bacterial load and contagiousness
Provide supportive care, including ensuring adequate hydration and nutrition
Monitor infants and severe cases closely for respiratory distress and apnea, often requiring hospitalization
Isolate infected individuals to prevent further spread, especially from vulnerable populations
Consider post-exposure prophylaxis for close contacts
age_group: All ages, especially infants and young children
content:
Whooping cough, also known as pertussis, is a highly contagious bacterial respiratory infection. It typically begins with cold-like symptoms, followed by severe coughing fits that can last for weeks or months, often ending with a characteristic 'whoop' sound during inhalation. This disease can be particularly serious and life-threatening for unvaccinated infants.
Symptoms: Runny nose, Mild fever, Mild, occasional cough (initial), Severe coughing fits, High-pitched whoop sound during inhalation after coughing, Vomiting after coughing, Fatigue, Apnea (pauses in breathing, especially in babies)
Visual Signs: Severe, rapid coughing fits, Vomiting after coughing episodes, Characteristic 'whooping' sound during inhalation, Periods of not breathing (apnea) in infants, Cyanosis (bluish skin due to lack of oxygen) during severe coughing

description: Diphtheria is a serious bacterial infection caused by Corynebacterium diphtheriae, primarily affecting the nose and throat, but can also involve the skin. It can lead to a tough, leathery pseudomembrane in the throat, which can block the airway and cause severe complications like heart and nerve damage.
visual_indicators: grey or white pseudomembrane in the throat
future_warnings: bleeding problems due to low platelets
immediate_actions: Administer diphtheria antitoxin (DAT)
Administer antibiotics (e.g., penicillin or erythromycin)
Ensure airway patency and provide respiratory support
Provide supportive care for complications
age_group: All age groups, especially unvaccinated children and adults
content:
Diphtheria is a serious bacterial infection caused by Corynebacterium diphtheriae, primarily affecting the nose and throat, but can also involve the skin. It can lead to a tough, leathery pseudomembrane in the throat, which can block the airway and cause severe complications like heart and nerve damage.
Symptoms: sore throat, fever, barking cough
Visual Signs: grey or white pseudomembrane in the throat, swollen neck (bull neck), skin lesions

description: Tetanus, also known as lockjaw, is a serious bacterial infection caused by Clostridium tetani, characterized by painful muscle spasms. These spasms typically begin in the jaw and spread throughout the body, lasting for several minutes and occurring frequently for three to four weeks. This uncommon disease requires immediate hospital treatment.
visual_indicators: Risus sardonicus (sustained spasm of facial muscles)
future_warnings: Fractured bones due to severe spasms
immediate_actions: Immediate hospitalization for treatment
Wound debridement to remove bacteria
Administration of Tetanus Immunoglobulin (TIG)
Antibiotics (e.g., metronidazole) to kill bacteria
Muscle relaxants (e.g., benzodiazepines) to control spasms
Supportive care, including respiratory support if needed
Tetanus vaccination (Tdap, DTaP, Td) for prevention and post-exposure prophylaxis
content:
Tetanus, also known as lockjaw, is a serious bacterial infection caused by Clostridium tetani, characterized by painful muscle spasms. These spasms typically begin in the jaw and spread throughout the body, lasting for several minutes and occurring frequently for three to four weeks. This uncommon disease requires immediate hospital treatment.
Symptoms: Muscle spasms, Lockjaw (trismus), Fever, Sweating, Headache, Trouble swallowing, High blood pressure, Fast heart rate
Visual Signs: Generalized muscle spasms, Lockjaw (inability to open mouth), Opisthotonus (arching of the back), Risus sardonicus (sustained spasm of facial muscles)

description: Poliomyelitis, or polio, is a highly contagious viral disease that can cause paralysis and even death. It spreads through contact with infected stool or respiratory droplets, primarily affecting the nervous system. While many cases are asymptomatic or mild, severe forms can lead to lifelong disability.
visual_indicators: Paralysis (inability to move parts of the body)
future_warnings: Post-polio syndrome (delayed muscle weakness years after initial infection)
immediate_actions: Supportive care (e.g., pain management, rest)
Physical therapy to manage paralysis
Respiratory support if breathing muscles are affected
age_group: Mainly children under 5, but unvaccinated individuals of any age are at risk
content:
Poliomyelitis, or polio, is a highly contagious viral disease that can cause paralysis and even death. It spreads through contact with infected stool or respiratory droplets, primarily affecting the nervous system. While many cases are asymptomatic or mild, severe forms can lead to lifelong disability.
Symptoms: Asymptomatic (in most cases), Sore throat, Fever, Fatigue, Nausea, Headache, Neck stiffness, Paresthesia (tingling/prickling sensation)
Visual Signs: Paralysis (inability to move parts of the body), Muscle weakness
